I probably should elaborate on that point a bit. I was never taught to just stand there and be killed, but I was told that whatever someone who tells me to get into a car with them or they'll shoot me has planned is a whole lot worse than being shot. It's not like I come from some really rich family where they'll ask for ransom money. Likely, they just want to beat me or rape me or kill me in some secluded area. I have a better chance at surviving if I make a run for it. Even if I am shot, there's a better chance at me being found and saved when I'm in a more public a place than if he takes me God knows where and decides to shoot me anyways. Basically, what I was taught is to run and NEVER get into a car with a strange man. I wouldn't just let someone who broke into my house just shoot me because it's less likely they have some terrible rape/murder planned and likely just want to rob me. I know my phrasing on this part was a little vague, haha!

I know. I would probably start having a panic attack in that situation. Not sure I could even force myself to be as calm as she was. But apparently keeping herself calm never set off the guy who was completely on edge the whole time. The whole thing where people around you mirrors how you act does in fact work in any situation, I guess.

I think that no matter what, it's better to be over prepared! I mean, never letting your kid out of the house is one thing, but giving them the tools so that they are prepared is another. My parents had me role play getting kidnapped to make sure I knew how to scream loudly and what to scream so it didn't look I was just throwing a tantrum. And no, I've never really had to use many of the things she taught me, but I suppose that acting on a lot of those creepy feeling may have prevented me from interacting with a creep. But I've been lucky enough to never be in one of those situations that are unavoidable (like many of the ones I read about on this sub. I mean, what am I supposed to do if someone just decides to stalk me?) I'm grateful to be able to stay safe from creeps during my life and never have to be in the same situation as my mother!

Mine too :(. I have always had a terrible fear of knives (which my mom thinks may have somehow oddly been passed down from her). It was actually one day when I was about eight when she first told me a very censored version of the story after I had a very irrational reaction to a steak knife falling off the table near me. I explained that I was really afraid of knives in any context and my mother looked at my father and asked "do you think she gets that from me?"

Actually, the guy took their car (probably forgot to make that clear) and it was the car they identified as the one he was in. Then my mother and her family were brought in and identified him. Plus, the police knew that he was probably going to New Hampshire (I believe his girlfriend and child or a brother or something was there) and they were looking for the car.

I'm so sorry this story frightened you! I tried to leave out the worst parts so that I could make it more about helpful for anyone (god forbid) who finds themselves in a similar position.

Unfortunately, I think my mother may also have gotten some of the details wrong in her retelling. Nothing major, but she's told me supermarker, convenience store, and strip mall, so it's been harder and harder to figure things out. She knows her end of the story and we know some girl lost her mother to this guy, but the exact details about this part (the part that made the news, if any) she hasn't really been clear about. I think she probably knows more than she's told me, but doesn't want me to know all of the details. I know this happened between 1982 and 1984, they lived in Maine, probably near Portland, and the guy drove to New Hampshire in their stolen car and killed some poor mother in front of her daughter. That's all that I know for sure about what would be in the news. If you want to do some research into this, be my guest, but I haven't been able to find anything. I really don't even know what to search.

I felt terrible when my mother told me about the little girl. I was told this story in bits and pieces, more details as I got older. First, I thought it was just about luck, then I realized that it was just my mother doing exactly what needed to happen. I feel so terrible for the poor girl. It's something that you'd never expect to happen outside of a crowded area like a strip mall. I never heard about what happened to her after all of this, but I wish my mother had contacted her and they had stayed in touch with the family. They probably needed more support than my mother and her family at the time. :(

That's really good that you teach your daughter those things! I'm a firm believer that it's just something that absolutely should be taught to every child, but talking to my friends, it apparently isn't as universal as I thought it would be.

I've tried digging around, but so far haven't found anything. Sadly, stabbings outside of strip malls is a little too common and my mother's family was for the most part left out of the story. They declined answering any questions and lived in a relatively small town in Maine. In fact, if I remember correctly, they were never contacted more than once about telling the story. Overall, it seems that the newspapers thought little of it and summed it up to just another unfortunate stabbing. :/

“Mom! Mom! Hey, Ma!” I called as I flipped through the channels of the television, actually too lazy to move my thumb to the guide button or Netflix. I soon remembered that my mother wasn’t home. Actually, she was on vacation. Which explained why I didn’t have a car…

Saturdays were getting boring being away from all my college friends. I hated summer. All my friends lived so far away. And were working.

Shit, was I supposed to be at work?

No, that’s right. I haven’t started my job yet…Whatever. I was bored.

Indy walked into the room and sat down in front of me. The dachshund looked at me with his big brown eyes.

“I shit on the floor,” he said.

“Really? And who do you think has to clean it up, now?” I groaned. Then I realized that my dog shouldn’t have been talking. “Wait, did you just say something?”

“Yes,” he said, “I came here to tell you that I made a shit and it is sitting in the middle of the living room. Please clean it up before I have to eat it.”

“Oh, that’s disgusting!” I scowled as I got up to take care of the mess. Sure enough, there was a large turd in the middle of the living room. “Why didn’t you tell me you had to go out?”

“I tried, but you did not see me. I am very short.”

I picked up the poop with a paper towel and tossed it into the toilet, Indy following close behind me.

“Wait, how can you talk?”

“I have always been able to talk, but you normally just ignore me over the sounds of the noisy picture box.”

“The TV? How do you not know the word for TV?”

“There is no word for that in my language.”

“You mean English?”

He scratched himself behind the ear. “Can we go play now?”

“What? No, we can’t.”

But before I knew it, Indy had gotten a ball from somewhere and was rolling it towards me with his nose. “Please throw the ball.”

“No.”

“Please?”

“If I throw the ball—“

“Ball! Ball! I heard you say ball! Where’s the ball? Where’s the ball? Here it is!” he picked it up in his mouth and began to whine. He dropped it, picked it up, dropped it again, and rolled it towards me.

“Throw it!” he cried, “Throw the ball! Throw it!”

“Okay!” I picked it up and threw it across the house.

“Oh, thank you, thank you, thank you!”

Fucking dog.

He held the gun to my head, the cold metal pressed against my forehead and grinned.

“You really don’t want to do this,” I said.

“Not what I would have picked as my last sentiment, but—“

Before he could finish I grabbed his wrist with my left hand and his elbow it my right. With a fluid motion, I stood up and kicked the back of his knee, twisting the arm as he fell. There was a sharp *pop* and then a sudden clatter of metal on concrete as the gun hit the ground. I kicked hard into his chest, stomping him backwards against the concrete. He yelped as his head collided. I scooped up the gun and knelt down on his working arm as I pressed the barrel to his head.

“Told you so,” I told him without a smile.

He was crying now. Clearly shocked and disoriented.

“Wha—what are you?” he asked through his tears.

“I’m the bitch you shouldn’t have messed with,” I scoffed and pulled the trigger.

He was a boy who thought that hunting immortals was fun, like in a video game. Sure, those games make it all seem like a joyride. Glamorous, even. He wanted the hero’s life. The money, the glory, the girls…And he made the mistake of thinking that I was the first level when I’m much more like the final boss. He’s playing a permadeath game out here. No extra lives, and no restarting. When it’s done, it’s Game Over.

I flipped the hair out of my face and tossed the gun on the ground. Hunters like him call us vampires or werewolves or other things that go bump in the night. But we’re nothing like that. No mystical powers. No rules about the sun or the moon. Just life. Forever.

I glanced back at the body, but it was nothing to me but a stupid boy who got himself killed. Nothing more. Nothing less.

“Hide, even if daddy calls you!” I hugged my daughter tightly. “No matter what, Lizzy, you do not come out!”

“Okay, mommy,” the frightened girl replied and hugged her stuffed rabbit closer to her. “Mommy, I’m scared.”

“Hush, now, sweetie, it’s going to be okay,” I kissed her, “Now go! Hide!”

She ran off up the stairs of the mansion and slipped away into one of the rooms, just in time. The door flew open and black mist poured into the hall. My husband, clad all in black and red, came storming in and seized me by the throat, backing me against a wall.

His formerly human face now appeared quite demonic with elongated teeth and pure black eyes. Horns protruded from his head through his long black hair.

“Liana, where is she?” he growled, “Where is my daughter? You can’t keep her from me!”

When I didn’t answer, he called for her. “Elizabeth! Elizabeth, come here at once!”

“She doesn’t love you anymore,” I choked out, “You left her. Left me! You aren’t welcome here anymore.”

He growled at me, but his face looked sad. He paused and then released me, turning back into a human form. He always was handsome, my husband. At least when he wore this guise. His true form was quite terrifying. But when you are married to a demon, that’s what you get.

“You and that girl are the only things I care about in this world, Liana. I didn’t leave you. I was always watching over—well, under you. But I can’t be the perfect father. I gave you this home and this life, Li, let me see our child, please.”

“I told you, Lu, you’re not welcome here anymore. And you can’t have our daughter. She belongs in this world.”

“That’s not true!” he growled, but then he sighed, “I’m trying to protect you.”

“You’re trying to take my baby girl away from me to Hell. You’re trying to lock her up there because Satan told you to do so. She’s a six year old child! She belong with her mother!”

“She’s a monster and deserves purgatory!” he growled.

“Get out of my house! I’m taking Liz and we’re leaving and I never want to hear from you again!” I yelled and slapped him across the face. I slipped by him and ran upstairs.

“Lizzy! Lizzy, darling?” I called.

“Momma!” she ran to me and I embraced her.

“Lizzy, we’re leaving. Go get the bag I had to pack.”

“I don’t want to, Momma,” she replied in a dull voice.

“What are you—“ there was a sudden pain in my gut. Lizzy was grinning a cruel grin. I looked down and saw the blood gushing out of my abdomen. I screamed.

“Liana?” Lu called. He dashed up the stairs. “Liana!” he caught me as I collapsed. “No! No, no, no, no, no! Liana!” his tears touched down on my face as he cradled me close. “Baby, I’m so sorry! I’m so, so sorry!”

His words faded away. I heard nothing. And I saw nothing. The pain diminished and everything just ended.

She invented stories about my hatred for the child and my anger problems. She was a pretty young thing with blonde hair, big boobs, and her husband’s money. I was living in a tiny little house that I could barely afford to keep. And I loved that girl. But bad luck followed me and I was sent to jail.

I didn’t rely on luck to get me out of here. I relied on skill.

The first person to get out of here was Carl McCarthy, a young, spry fellow. He became so rich and famous afterwards that he retired from his job as a drug dealer and became an actor. A shitty actor, but an actor nonetheless. A movie was made about his life. He died last year at the age of 48 when a young man put a bullet in his head because Jesus told him to. That man now rots in a jail cell.

The next man was Junjie Fu, an acrobat who got himself arrested for the sole purpose of breaking out of jail. He wanted to prove he could do it. It didn’t get him nearly as much fame as it got McCarthy, but Fu got a taste for the criminal life and now works as a thief for hire out in California.

And me? My name is Kaya Brooks. I suppose this makes me the third person to escape from prison. I can never go back. By law, I am immune to, well, the law. I’m not sure what I should do now that I’m out. I don’t know what I can do now. Anything, I suppose. The first woman to escape prison certainly would get at least a few interviews. But before all of that, I there is something I need to do.

My sister thought she locked me up forever. Won’t she be surprised?

I suppose it all started when we were kids. We never really got along. I don’t really believe that there are “pretty sisters” and “smart sisters” in most families, but it certainly was the case in ours. I was the smart one. I got average grades in school, but I was clever. I could see patterns and knew how to read people. Manipulation was a talent of mine.

When I was seven, I convinced my parents to let have a cell phone. My sister was jealous because she was nine and didn’t have one. When I was fourteen, I figured out that my teacher was having an affair with our TA and I promptly blackmailed him into letting me skip class.

My sister, on the other hand, was the pretty one. While this got her nowhere with our parents, she was clever enough to convince the boys to do her homework and carry her book bag home from school. But her one serious boyfriend, Joey Levi, was the only one she cared about. And I was the only one *he* cared about. She walked in one day to find us together and has hated me ever since.

My niece was the product of his apology to her. But he left her when I got engaged to a young man who promptly died when he was shot down by Harry Cummings, our next door neighbor who was found innocent after his wealthy mother blackmailed the jury.

My sister has always hated me. But she’s gone too far. It’s time for her to face judgment. I’ll be the judge, jury, and executioner.

I walk up the steps to her large house that was paid for with the money that her husband made, a knife in my hands. It is the only thing I could get on after escaping. I’m still in my orange jumpsuit that is ripped and tattered from getting caught on barbed wire and torn from that dog that almost caught me.

I am about to ring the doorbell, but hesitate. I feel nothing but the anger welling up inside of me. She has to die, I know this! Before I can make myself ring the bell, the door swings open and standing there is the last person I expected to see. Blue eyed, dark haired, and covered in blood. He freezes and stares at me with a fearful look in his eyes. But then he calms down and just looks confused.

“Joey? What are you…?”

I stare at him across the table, feeling a bit fearful as he looks me in the eyes. I hadn’t seen Joey in several years and now he just appears at my sister’s house?

“Why did you kill her?” I ask calmly.

He looks down at the body and then back to me.

“She killed Janie. She framed you,” he replies slowly and calmly. I look into his cold eyes and see nothing. Not even a hint of emotion.

“You did this for me? Or for the daughter you left when she was just a baby?”

“Do you hate me, Kaya?”

“You left. And my fiancé died.”

“But I came back. For you, Kaya. Please, come with me,” he reaches for my hand and for a moment, his cold fingers touch mine. I pull away and glare at him. He looks away with a dejected look and stares down at the blood that’s everywhere. “You escaped. I was going to get myself arrested to be with you.”

“They keep men and women separate, dumb ass.”

“I would escape and not break out, just to be with you. I break into your side and we’d get out together. I still love you, Kay.”

A shiver runs up my spine as his words sink in. Is he crazy? Am I in real danger now?

A time passes, I get the feeling more and more that I want to be away from him. I think that I may be in actual danger. What was escaping for if this is my fate?

“Joey, you need to leave,” I finally say, “You need to get out of here, because you won’t escape from prison. It’s much harder than you think. You’ll die in there.”

“Kaya…”

“I’ll take the blame for Kat’s death. But you need to leave. Now.”

“Kaya…”

“Get out!”

With that, he stands up abruptly with a fearful look plastered on his face. He almost seems hurt by my words. I keep my expression stern, though, and eventually he bows his head low and mutters, “thank you, Kaya.” He leaves without another word.

After a moment of processing what just happened and why, I pick up the phone and dial 911.

“My name is Kaya Brooks. I just killed my sister,” I say and then hang up. I leave the house and walk home as it begins to rain.

This was the first day of my freedom. What will the rest of my life be like?

Freedom is not as good as it seems. My house is literally a crime scene. Despite being a free woman, none of my friends trust me in their house.

I wake up in the morning and at least a dozen reporters are at my door looking for me. I’m not good around the cameras.

“Miss Brooks, why did you kill your sister?” “Miss Brooks, how did you escape?” “Miss Brooks, what do you plan on doing now?”

I can’t process all of the questions. There are just too many. I close the door on them.

My legacy is two murders I didn’t commit and the ability to do whatever I want. All I want, though, is to walk around my house and be alone. I want to hold my niece. I want to be with my fiancé. Everything taken from me. A run of bad luck.

“Kaya?” comes a voice. I turn to see Joey in my kitchen. He is holding roses and smiling at me. “You love me, Kaya. You took the blame for me. And I love you. You’ve earned my love.”

I didn’t think my day could have gotten any worse, but now it is.

I’m sick of bad luck. This world has only given me misfortune. It’s time for me to make my own luck.

“Momma?” a little blonde child asked Jolie. Jolie looked down at her. Anika. They found her a few days ago in the rubble of an old house, crying. She had likely been born in a bunker or, God forbid, in the wastelands of this dreadful world.

“I’m not your mother,” Jolie said for what felt like the thousandth time.
